blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Overdispersion means the variance of a count exceeds its mean, beyond what the Poisson model allows. Negative binomial (NB) regression adds one parameter, α ≥ 0, so that

Var(Y) = μ + αμ².

When α = 0 this is the Poisson model. Some software, R among it, reports θ = 1/α instead and writes the variance as μ + μ²/θ (Zeileis et al., 2008).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Counts often cluster more than a pure Poisson process predicts, because units differ in unmeasured ways or because cases cause cases. The Poisson model then treats the data as more informative than they are: SEs too small, CIs too narrow, p-values too small. NB regression lets the data estimate the extra variation. The exponentiated coefficient keeps its meaning (IRR with an offset), but its value and SE are re-estimated.

Checking for overdispersion. A rough check is the dispersion statistic: the Pearson χ² of the Poisson fit, Σ(observed − fitted)²/fitted over the units (recall Pearson’s statistic, §10.6), divided by its residual degrees of freedom. Values near 1 are consistent with Poisson variation; values well above 1 suggest overdispersion. The residual deviance (a likelihood-based measure of lack of fit, defined in §15.1.1) ÷ df is used the same way. These are rules of thumb, not tests. A formal comparison is the likelihood-ratio test of the Poisson against the NB model (α = 0 against α > 0), which compares their log-likelihoods (Zeileis et al., 2008).

Excess zeros. Sometimes there are more zeros than either model expects, because part of the population cannot have the event at all. Cigarettes smoked per day is 0 for every non-smoker, whatever their other characteristics. Two families of models deal with this (Zeileis et al., 2008):

  • A zero-inflated model is a mixture: a “structural zero” group (always 0) plus a Poisson or NB count group that can also produce zeros. A logistic part models membership of the zero group.
  • A hurdle model has two parts: a binary model for zero vs any positive count, and a truncated count model (one that allows only counts of 1 or more) for the positive counts.

Both models have two sets of predictors: one for the zeros and one for the counts.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The malaria model of §13.5 has a Pearson χ² of 23.7 on 8 residual df: dispersion 2.97. The residual deviance, 24.37 on 8 df, gives 3.05. The village counts vary about three times as much as the Poisson model assumes, as the contagion argument of §13.5 predicted.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Dispersion statistic = 2.97 (Pearson), 3.05 (deviance). Both well above 1.
  2. The NB fit gives θ = 18.7, so α = 1/18.7 = 0.053.
  3. For a village near water with mean 38.2 cases, Poisson variance = 38.2; NB variance = 38.2 + 0.053 × 38.2² = 116.2, about three times as large.
  4. Likelihood-ratio test of α = 0: LR = 4.67; against χ²₁, p = 0.031. Because α cannot be negative, α = 0 lies on the boundary of its possible values, and the correct null distribution is a 50:50 mixture of a point mass at 0 and χ²₁ (StataCorp, 2023). The p-value is therefore half: p = 0.015.
  5. NB IRR = 2.47 (95% CI 1.70 to 3.60), against the Poisson 2.30 (1.83 to 2.89). On the log scale the interval is about 1.6 times as wide.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
# dispersion statistic
sum(residuals(p1, "pearson")^2) / p1$df.residual
library(MASS)
nb <- glm.nb(cases ~ near_water + offset(log(population)), data = ml)
exp(cbind(IRR = coef(nb), confint.default(nb)))
c(theta = nb$theta, alpha = 1 / nb$theta)
lr <- as.numeric(2 * (logLik(nb) - logLik(p1)))
c(LR = lr, p = pchisq(lr, 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
[1] 2.968425
                  IRR       2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept) 0.0083963 0.006361756 0.01108151
near_water  2.4748383 1.701596933 3.59945683
      theta       alpha 
18.70345592  0.05346605 
        LR          p 
4.67230655 0.03065273

The first line is the dispersion statistic of step 1. glm.nb returns the NB IRR, 2.47 (1.70 to 3.60), and θ = 18.7 (α = 0.053). The LR of 4.67 compares the two log-likelihoods; the printed p (0.031) uses χ²₁ and is halved to 0.015 for the boundary, step 4.

points.html: Poisson: Var = μ. NB: Var = μ + αμ² (some software reports θ = 1/α). Overdispersion ignored → SEs too small.
Dispersion statistic (Pearson χ²/df, or deviance/df) is a rough check; the LR test of α = 0 is the formal one (halve its χ²₁ p-value, because α = 0 is a boundary).
Switching to NB changes the coefficient values and SEs, not the meaning of exp(b).
An alternative is the quasi-Poisson model, which keeps the Poisson estimates and inflates the SEs by the estimated dispersion (Zeileis et al., 2008).
NB absorbs extra variation; it does not model transmission. With 10 villages, α is poorly estimated, and contagion is a reason to look at designs and models built for infectious disease.
More zeros than expected, from a group that cannot have the event: consider a zero-inflated or hurdle model.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 13.4

questions.prompt: A Poisson regression of malaria cases on “near standing water”, with log(village population) as an offset, gives exp(b) = 2.30. Is this a rate ratio or a count ratio? What would exp(b) be without the offset in these data, and why does it differ?
questions.answer: A rate ratio (incidence rate ratio): with the offset, the model is for log(cases/population). Villages near water have 2.30 times the malaria rate of the others (20.1 vs 8.74 per 1,000). Without the offset, exp(b) is the ratio of mean cases per village, 38.2/23.6 = 1.62. It is smaller because the villages near water have fewer people (9,500 vs 13,500 in total), so their counts understate their rate.

questions.prompt: A Poisson model shows clear overdispersion. What does switching to negative binomial regression change, and what does it leave unchanged?
questions.answer: It changes the variance assumption from Var = μ to Var = μ + αμ², so the model is fitted against a different likelihood. The coefficient estimates can shift somewhat (IRR 2.30 → 2.47 in the malaria data), and the SEs and CIs widen to reflect the extra variation (1.83–2.89 → 1.70–3.60), making tests more honest. The meaning of exp(b) is unchanged: still a rate ratio with an offset, a count ratio without.

questions.prompt: A Poisson model of monthly diarrhoea episodes has Pearson χ² = 40 on 10 residual df. Compute the dispersion statistic. If an NB fit gives α = 0.1, what variance does it imply for a child whose expected count is 2 episodes? For an expected count of 20?
questions.answer: Dispersion statistic = 40/10 = 4, well above 1: the counts vary about four times as much as the Poisson model allows (a rough check; confirm with the likelihood-ratio test of α = 0). NB variance = μ + αμ². μ = 2: 2 + 0.1 × 4 = 2.4 (close to Poisson). μ = 20: 20 + 0.1 × 400 = 60, three times the Poisson variance. Overdispersion under the NB model grows with the mean.
